topic: Japan was settled in the Paleolithic; the Jōmon foragers were followed by Yayoi rice farmers, and by the 5th century the Yamato kings ruled much of the islands.
Ideas from China and Korea (Buddhism, writing, law) shaped classical Japan; from the 12th century real power passed to warriors and the shoguns.
The Tokugawa shoguns kept peace and limited foreign contact for 250 years; the Meiji Restoration of 1868 then industrialised Japan at speed and made it an empire.
Expansion led to the Pacific War and defeat in 1945; post-war Japan became a constitutional democracy and one of the world's largest economies.

Prehistoric and ancient Japan: Humans reached Japan around 38,000–40,000 years ago; the Jōmon period (from about 14,000 BC) produced some of the world's oldest pottery.
The Yayoi period (from about 1000–300 BC) brought wet-rice farming, metalworking and newcomers from the Asian mainland.
In the Kofun period (3rd–6th centuries) great keyhole-shaped burial mounds mark the rise of the Yamato state.
Classical Japan: Buddhism arrived from the Korean kingdom of Baekje in the 6th century; the Asuka-period court adopted Chinese-style government, writing and law.
After defeat at Baekgang (663) and the Jinshin War (672), emperors such as Tenmu strengthened the state; the first histories, Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, were written.
The Nara period (710–794) had a permanent capital modelled on Chang'an; Emperor Shōmu built the great Buddha of Tōdai-ji.
In the Heian period (794–1185) the Fujiwara regents ran the court, and court literature flourished, above all Murasaki Shikibu's Tale of Genji.
Feudal Japan: After the Genpei War, Minamoto no Yoritomo set up the first shogunate at Kamakura (1192); warriors (samurai) now held real power.
Kamakura Japan repelled the Mongol invasions of 1274 and 1281.
The Ashikaga (Muromachi) shogunate weakened, and the Ōnin War (1467–77) began a century of civil war, the Sengoku period.
Oda Nobunaga, Toyotomi Hideyoshi and Tokugawa Ieyasu reunified Japan; Ieyasu's victory at Sekigahara (1600) settled it. Portuguese traders and missionaries arrived from 1543.
Early modern Japan: The Tokugawa shogunate ruled from Edo (Tokyo) for over 250 years of peace; society was fixed into four classes: samurai, farmers, artisans, merchants.
After the Shimabara Rebellion (1637–38) Christianity was banned and foreign contact was limited to the Dutch and Chinese at Nagasaki: the 'sakoku' policy.
Commodore Perry's American ships forced Japan open in 1853–54; the shogunate lost authority, and the Boshin War (1868–69) restored power to the emperor.
Modern Japan: The Meiji government abolished the samurai class (the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877 was their last stand), adopted a constitution (1889) and industrialised rapidly.
Japan defeated China (1894–95) and Russia (1904–05) and annexed Korea (1910), becoming an imperial power.
In the 1930s militarists took control: the invasion of Manchuria (1931) and war with China (from 1937) included atrocities such as the Nanjing Massacre.
Japan attacked Pearl Harbor in 1941 and surrendered in 1945 after the atomic bombings; under American occupation it adopted a pacifist constitution and later became an economic power.
Social conditions: Social rank grew sharper with rice farming in the Yayoi period and was formalised in the Tokugawa class system.
Modernisation after 1868 abolished legal classes and spread schooling.
Today Japan faces an ageing and shrinking population.
